verses.translation_literal: Of the sons of Korah, a psalm, a song. His foundation [is] in the mountains of holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of the sons of Korah, a song. His foundation stands upon the holy mountains.
verses.directors_commentary: Open with the title, not as a label to be mumbled but as a signature: this is a song belonging to the Korahites, the temple singers, and they are about to sing of the place where they serve. Then the first line drops the audience into mid-thought, with no name given: "his foundation." The suffix on yesudato is masculine, and the speaker deliberately leaves the antecedent open. Two readings are on offer, and the actor should know both. The first, the one KJV, ASV and Webster carry over unchanged and YLT keeps as 'His foundation', takes God as the founder: what the LORD has founded stands among holy mountains. The second, which Rashi and Metzudat David take, reads 'foundation' as the base of this psalm itself: the song's theme rests on the holy mountains. Note that the suffix cannot be Zion: Zion is feminine, and the psalm later says bah and yekhonneha for her. BBE settles the matter by inventing a noun ("this house"), which the Hebrew does not have. The plural 'mountains of holiness' is a construct chain, literally 'mountains of holiness'; a city on a ridge of hills (Zion and Moriah, as Radak reads it) is natural for a place whose neighbours were all defended by height. The KJV also turns the two title nouns into alternatives ("A Psalm or Song"); Hebrew simply sets 'a psalm, a song' side by side. KJV's verse 87:0 is the Hebrew's title and 87:1 its first clause, so the two numbers share one Hebrew verse.

philological_notes.note: 'His foundation': a feminine noun with a masculine 3rd-person suffix. The suffix is masculine, so it points not to Zion but either to God (the founder) or to the psalm and its theme. Both readings are old; the first is that of the English versions, the second that of Rashi and Metzudat David.
'In the mountains of holiness': plural, a construct chain with qodesh, 'set-apartness, holiness'. Radak reads the plural as Mount Zion with Mount Moriah, or as the surrounding hills.

verses.translation_literal: Loving [is] YHWH the gates of Zion, more than all the dwelling-places of Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD loves the gates of Zion. He loves them more than every dwelling of Jacob.
verses.directors_commentary:
A participle opens the line: 'loving is YHWH'. The Hebrew names the love before the beloved, and describes an ongoing state, not a past act. The KJV's 'loveth' is archaic but accurate; what it loses is that the love comes first, so the sentence leans toward its object like a hand reaching for a door.

The object is odd. The LORD loves not Zion but its gates. In an ancient walled city the gate was the courthouse, the marketplace and the place where elders sat; Radak notes that the sages and elders sat in the gates, and that this is why the gates stand for the city's people and their learning. The contrast, 'more than all the dwelling-places of Jacob', is deliberately provocative: Jacob's settlements, tent-camps and homes across the land, loved less. 'Dwellings' here is the word mishkenot, the plural of mishkan, the same root as the tabernacle, so the line sets a sanctuary-city against the whole country of ordinary tents. Malbim hears an insult the nations might make, that God loves only Zion, and turns it into praise. Play it as a statement of preference, not of rejection: Meiri and Metzudat David both stress that all Israel remains beloved.

philological_notes.note: 'Gates of Zion', the city's public face: judgment, trade and teaching took place there. Radak reads the gates as the elders and scholars who sit in them.
'Dwelling-places', plural of mishkan, 'tabernacle'; here the settlements of Jacob contrasted with the one city of the sanctuary.

verses.translation_literal: Glorious things [are] spoken in you, city of God. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Glorious things are said of you, city of God. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the poet turns and speaks to the city itself: 'you'. Until here Zion was an 'it'; from this line on she is addressed face to face. The shift should land in the voice, a drop in volume and a step closer.

The KJV 'spoken of thee' is fine as sense, but the Hebrew preposition is literally 'in': glorious things are spoken in you. The word translated 'glorious' is from the root kavod, weight or honour, and it is feminine plural and passive in form, so 'weighty, honoured things'. Rashi hears God himself as the speaker. Metzudat David reads it as what is said in her courts, where the Sanhedrin sits and studies Torah. Both are possible; the text does not say who speaks, so do not assign a speaker. 'City of God' uses 'Elohim', the common word for God and gods, which in a city full of rival shrines to other deities is a claim. Selah is a marker of a pause or a musical lift; its meaning is unknown, and it should be left untranslated and held as a rest.

philological_notes.note: A feminine plural participle from the root of 'weight, honour': things of weight, honoured things. The KJV 'glorious' is acceptable; YLT's 'honourable' is closer.
A marker of uncertain meaning, probably a musical or liturgical pause or lift. Left untranslated.

verses.translation_literal: I will cause to be remembered Rahab and Babylon to those who know me; behold, Philistia and Tyre with Cush: this one was born there.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will call to mind Rahab and Babylon before those who know me. And look: Philistia, and Tyre, and Cush alongside them. "This one was born there."
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns here from the city to the world, and the speaker lists the great powers like a herald reading names. Rahab is Egypt: the name means 'bluster, arrogance' and is used for Egypt elsewhere (Isa 30:7), with an echo of the chaos monster Rahab whom God crushes (Ps 89:11 [10]). Babylon is the power of the east, Philistia and Tyre are the neighbours to the west, and Cush is the Nile land south of Egypt. KJV's "Ethiopia" follows the old Greek and Latin habit; Cush is Nubia, upstream, not the modern state. So the names run in a circle round Israel, and the actor should deliver them as a sweep, with the surprise held for the last phrase: "this one was born there." Who is 'I'? Ibn Ezra and Radak make it the poet speaking to those who share his knowledge of Zion; Metzudat David makes it God, calling these peoples to mind. The Hebrew allows both, and the director must choose one voice for the performance. KJV's "this man was born there" adds "man" and "that"; the Hebrew has only zeh, 'this one', as a spoken line with no frame. And 'there' is disputed too: Rashi and Metzudat David hear it as Zion, the place these nations' people were born into, while Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri hear it as the nations themselves, where only now and then a sage is born. The phrase 'to those who know me' is lamed with a participle, not 'among': it is spoken to, or for, those who know the speaker. The refrain zeh yulad sham will return in verse 6; its tone should be set here.

philological_notes.note: A poetic name for Egypt, from a root meaning 'to be arrogant, to bluster'. It recalls the sea monster of Ps 89:11 and is used of Egypt in Isa 30:7. Not the woman Rahab of Jericho, whose name is spelled differently.

'To those who know me': preposition lamed, participle 'knowing', 1st-person suffix. Metzudat Zion glosses the participle as 'dear, beloved', as in Prov 7:4. Radak allows the suffix to refer to Zion or to the poet.

'This one was born there': a bare quoted line with no 'that', repeated in verses 5 and 6 with variations (bah, 'in her'; sham, 'there'). The place meant is Zion for Rashi and Metzudat David, the nations for Ibn Ezra and Radak.

verses.translation_literal: And of Zion it will be said, "A man and a man was born in her," and he, the Most High, will establish her.
verses.translation_dramatic: But of Zion it will be said: this one, and that one, was born in her. And the Most High himself will make her stand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn is in one small letter. 'And of Zion' begins with a lamed, 'concerning, of Zion', and the conjunction sets her against the foreign cities just listed. Of them, the poet said 'this one was born there'. Of Zion the claim is bigger.

The Hebrew 'ish ve'ish' is literally 'a man and a man'. English versions go three ways: 'this and that man' (KJV), 'each one' (YLT), 'this one and that one' (ASV). The sense is a repetition that means 'one after another, all of them' (Ibn Ezra: 'not this one alone'). The point is a count: elsewhere a notable person is born; here, citizens beyond number. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as a roll of scholars; the Targum names David and Solomon, which the Hebrew does not.

Then the last clause. 'And he' gives the sentence a stress that the KJV 'the highest himself' catches well. In Hebrew the pronoun is separate: 'and he will establish her, Elyon'. The title Elyon, 'Most High', was an old name for God in Canaan, which here takes the place of the divine name. The verb is kun, to set firm; it echoes the foundation of verse 1, so the psalm closes a ring: she has a foundation, and God himself will make it hold.

philological_notes.note: 'A man and a man': a doubled noun with a distributive sense, 'one and another', 'every single one'. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'not this one alone'.
'He will establish her', a polel verb, to fix firmly, with the feminine object suffix pointing to the city. It echoes 'foundation' in verse 1.
'Most High', an ancient divine title; here it stands as an apposition to the pronoun 'he'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read the clause as 'and the Most High, he, will establish her'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH will count, in the writing of peoples: this one was born there. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD himself will count them, even as he inscribes the peoples. And of one he will say: "This one was born there." Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse in which the speaker steps back and lets YHWH be named in the third person, and the actor should hear the change of register: after the 'I' of verse 4, the LORD is now a distant clerk of the nations, writing and counting. The picture is a census. Ancient states kept registers of citizens and of peoples, and to be enrolled was to belong. The verb yispor can mean 'count' or 'recount, tell' (Meiri reads it as telling); bikhtov is an infinitive, 'in the writing of', so the line says, 'when he writes the peoples, he will count'. Radak takes the writing as God's decree. Rashi finds the verse transposed, with Selah belonging at the end of 'peoples', and has the LORD sorting out the Israelites swallowed among the nations; Metzudat David agrees. The KJV's "when he writeth up the people" turns the infinitive into a finite verb and makes 'peoples' singular, and it adds "that" and "man" to what is a bare spoken line: "this one was born there." The 'there' is again open, Zion or the nations, as in verse 4. Selah closes the verse and, with it, a pause for the musicians: hold the silence before the final verses.

philological_notes.note: 'He will count': imperfect of safar, 'to count, to recount'. The sense of tallying a register fits the setting; Meiri hears the sense 'tell'.
Infinitive construct of katav with the prefix bet: 'in the writing of, when he writes'. It governs 'peoples', so God is the writer. Radak understands the writing as the divine decree.

verses.translation_literal: And singers, like pipers: all my springs [are] in you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the singers, and the pipers with them, all sing: every spring I have is in you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last verse has no verb at all, which is why English translations disagree on what happens in it. 'And singers, like pipers' is all the Hebrew gives, and then the surprising closing line. A good performance leaves the gap open and lets the music fill it.

The tricky word is the second one. It is a participle that either means 'pipers', from the root for 'pierce', the instrument being a pierced reed (so KJV 'players on instruments', Radak and Metzudat Zion citing Isa 5:12), or 'dancers', from the root for 'whirl' (so ASV, BBE; Rashi cites Judg 21:23). Both are good: in an ancient procession the singers, the flute players and the dancers moved together. The little prefix 'like' (ke-) is usually understood as 'as well as', so the singers and the pipers alike. The KJV's 'shall be there' is added, not in the text.

The final clause is a shock of intimacy after the roll call of nations. 'My springs' (ma'yanai) is poetry of water in a land of drought: a spring is the source of life, and a city with a spring does not die. Whose springs? The pilgrims', who sing. Rashi reads 'my innards', Radak 'my thoughts and attention', Malbim 'springs of salvation'. The Hebrew has the plural 'my springs', so the singer's whole inner source is located in Zion, the one place where the people's life wells up.

philological_notes.note: Either 'pipers' (a pierced reed, from the root meaning to pierce) or 'dancers' (from a root meaning to whirl). Radak and Metzudat Zion give 'players on the flute'; Rashi, 'dancers'.
'My springs', with a first-person suffix. The root is 'eye, spring'. Read as the source of life and joy; Rashi takes it as 'my innards', Radak as 'my thoughts'.
